heading: Desktop App Architecture
text: The Worklog Studio desktop app is built with Flutter and Dart, which is what lets a single codebase ship native builds for both macOS and Windows. State management uses the BLoC pattern, with dependency injection via get_it/injectable. Data is stored locally in a SQLite database (via sqflite) — there is no backend server or cloud sync for the desktop app today. The app integrates with the OS at a few points: a system tray/menu bar presence (via window_manager and tray_manager), and a native auto-updater (Sparkle) that checks for and installs new versions.

heading: Landing Page & AI Chat Assistant Architecture
text: This landing page is a Next.js (App Router) + React + TypeScript site, styled with Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel. The AI chat assistant on this page is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system: visitor questions are embedded and matched against a small, hand-authored knowledge base (this same set of markdown content) using cosine similarity, and Google's Gemini model generates the answer from only the matched content — it does not answer from general knowledge, and it will say it doesn't know rather than guess if nothing relevant is found.

heading: How Worklog Studio Compares
text:
Worklog Studio was built after using and evaluating several other time trackers, each missing something:

- **Top Tracker (Toptal)**: has a floating always-on-top window and hotkey task switching, but no way to add comments or descriptions to a task.
- **My Hours**: supports task descriptions, but the free tier doesn't allow editing entries, and it has no desktop app (browser/PWA only).
- **RescueTime**: fully paid, oriented around passive activity tracking rather than an explicit start/stop timer workflow.
- **Clockspot**: fully paid, built for company employee time tracking with manual entry, web-only.

Worklog Studio's current differentiators are: free to use, local-first storage (no account, no server-side data), per-task and per-entry comments/descriptions, and a single-keystroke start with no mandatory project setup. It does not currently have Top Tracker's floating-window/hotkey workflow — that's a future idea, not a shipped feature (see the future-ideas content). It also deliberately leaves out invoicing, billable rates, and team/client management, which the tools above are partly built around.

heading: Contributing
text: Worklog Studio is open source (MIT license) at github.com/vavilov2212/wl-studio, and outside contributions via GitHub issues and pull requests are welcome. There isn't a formal contributing process yet — no CONTRIBUTING.md, style guide, or review checklist — so the most useful first step is opening an issue to discuss a change before submitting a pull request.

heading: Projects, Tasks, and Time Entries
text:
Worklog Studio's data model has three core concepts:

- **Project**: a top-level container for related work, with a status of open, done, or archived.
- **Task**: belongs to a project, has its own title and description, and a status of open, done, or archived.
- **Time Entry**: a recorded span of time (start, optional end) that can be linked to a project and task, and can carry a free-text comment. A running time entry has no end time yet; a stopped one does.

This model is intentionally simple — no client/billing fields, no team assignment — matching the product's focus on solo, personal time tracking rather than agency or team billing workflows.

text: Terms like "Flow Score," "Deep Work hours," and "Efficiency %" appear in the landing page's Focus Analytics preview, but they are illustrative placeholder concepts for a planned feature, not metrics the app currently computes. There's no real definition for these yet — when that feature is built, this content will be updated with the actual definitions.

heading: Seamless Integrations
text: Worklog Studio syncs automatically with GitHub (commits and PRs) and Linear (issues and workspace tasks) today. Google Calendar and Notion integrations are planned.

heading: Frictionless Tracking
text: Start logging a deep work session with a single keystroke or click. No complex forms or project setup required — the interface stays out of the way until it's needed.

heading: Projects, Tasks, and Time Entries
text: Worklog Studio organizes work around three concepts: a Project contains Tasks, and a Time Entry records a span of time against a Project and Task (or neither, for ad-hoc tracking). Each time entry can carry a free-text comment, and each task has its own description field — so you can capture what you were actually doing or thinking at each stage of the work, not just a task title. This comment/description support is a deliberate design choice: it was the single biggest gap the author found in other time trackers before building Worklog Studio (see the "Why Worklog Studio" content for the full comparison).

heading: Local-First Storage
text: All time-tracking data is stored locally on the user's machine in a SQLite database file — there's no account, no server-side sync, and no remote storage of personal data. The app also writes timestamped local backup snapshots of that database file automatically, so a user can recover recent data if something goes wrong (see the troubleshooting content for details).

heading: Exploratory Ideas (Not on the Committed Roadmap)
text:
These are ideas the author is considering, not committed features — they should not be presented as "coming soon" or planned with any timeline. For committed plans, see the roadmap content instead.

- **Floating always-on-top window with hotkey task switching**: inspired by Top Tracker, lets a user switch tasks without leaving their current app. Not yet implemented.
- **Integrations with Notion, Jira, and Slack**: parsing tasks from those tools automatically instead of manual entry. Not yet started — only GitHub and Linear integrations are currently shipped.
- **AI-assisted nudges**: the app noticing context (e.g. switching from an IDE to a browser) and proactively asking things like "are you still working on this?" or suggesting a description update. Purely an idea at this stage.
- **Cloud/SaaS web version**: a web-based version with sign-in and remote data storage, as an alternative to today's fully local-first desktop app. Just a loose idea, not scoped or scheduled.

heading: Installing Worklog Studio
text:
Worklog Studio downloads as a zip archive for both macOS and Windows — there's no installer/setup wizard yet (that's a planned improvement), so after downloading, the user extracts the zip and runs the app directly.

Because the app isn't notarized by Apple or signed with a Windows EV certificate, first launch can trigger OS warnings that look alarming but are expected:

- **macOS**: Gatekeeper will warn that the app is from an "unidentified developer." Right-click the app and choose "Open" (instead of double-clicking), or allow it via System Settings → Privacy & Security.
- **Windows**: SmartScreen will show a "Windows protected your PC" warning. Click "More info," then "Run anyway."

These warnings are a known rough edge, especially for non-technical users, and the author is aware of it — a proper signed installer/setup wizard is a planned future improvement, not yet built.

heading: Why Worklog Studio Was Built
text:
Worklog Studio was built out of personal frustration with existing time-tracking tools, not as a market-research exercise. The author tried several tools first: Top Tracker (by Toptal), My Hours, RescueTime, and Clockspot.

Top Tracker came closest — it has a floating always-on-top window and hotkey-driven task switching, which the author found genuinely useful for staying in flow without alt-tabbing to a separate app. But it has no way to attach a description or comment to a task, which matters a lot for a workflow built around switching between different stages or objectives within the same task.

My Hours covers the comment/description gap that Top Tracker misses, but lacks the floating-window/hotkey workflow. Its free tier also doesn't allow editing existing entries. RescueTime and Clockspot are paid, aimed more at company/team time tracking, and RescueTime's timer-based workflow wasn't clear or central to the product.

More broadly, the tools the author evaluated were either subscription-only from day one, feature-heavy with invoicing/team/paywall functionality the author didn't need, or stored data on a remote server when local-first storage (with optional sync to something like Google Drive) would be preferable for a personal tool. Open-source alternatives existed too, but were similarly cluttered for a single-person, personal-use case.

Worklog Studio is the author's attempt at the tool that was missing: simple, free, local-first, and focused on frictionless single-keystroke tracking with per-task comments — without invoicing, team management, or paywalled core features.

heading: Value Proposition
text: Worklog Studio is a minimal, distraction-free desktop time logger for professionals, developers, and creators who prioritize deep work and flow states. It avoids the high-friction, form-heavy UI of traditional time trackers — no project setup wizard, no mandatory categories or tags before you can start a timer.

heading: Target Audience
text: Worklog Studio is built for engineers, designers, and founders who want to understand where their time actually goes without breaking their concentration to log it. It's deliberately not aimed at agencies or teams that need invoicing, billable-rate tracking, or client reporting — those features are out of scope by design, not yet-missing.

heading: If Something Goes Wrong
text:
If the app crashes or behaves unexpectedly, report it on GitHub Issues at github.com/vavilov2212/wl-studio/issues, or email the author directly at vavilov2212@gmail.com. Include your OS and version, and steps to reproduce if possible.

If your tracked data looks wrong or missing, Worklog Studio automatically keeps timestamped local backup snapshots of its SQLite database file alongside the live one — check for a recent backup before assuming data is permanently lost.
